html:
A huge and richly carved church in Constantinople, built from 524 to 527 by Anicia Juliana, a noblewoman descended from the emperors of the house of Theodosius. Until Hagia Sophia it was the largest church in the city.

Juliana built it to show off her imperial blood at a time when the new emperors, Justin I and Justinian, were upstarts from the Balkans. A long poem carved around the nave praised her family. The stone carving was lavish, with vines, peacocks and patterns borrowed from Sasanian Persian art. It may also have had an early dome, and some scholars see it as the rival that pushed Justinian to build Hagia Sophia.

Little is known of its later history. It was in ruins by the 12th century, and crusaders took carved pieces to Venice after 1204. The site was found in 1960 during roadworks in Istanbul and dug in the 1960s.
sum: A huge and richly carved church in Constantinople, built from 524 to 527 by Anicia Juliana, a noblewoman descended from the emperors of the house of Theodosius. Until Hagia Sophia it was the largest church in the city.
